questions.prompt: To search for unrecorded sales, which direction is most appropriate?

choices.text: Vouch only recorded sales to invoices.
Inspect only the largest recorded receivable.
Trace independently selected shipping documents to the sales journal.
Recalculate the audit fee.

questions.explanation: Start outside the possibly incomplete records and trace inward; selecting only recorded items cannot reliably identify omissions.

questions.prompt: Vouching recorded inventory items to the warehouse most directly addresses which assertion?

choices.text: Completeness of all unrecorded inventory.
Legal ownership in every case.
Net realizable value automatically.
Existence.

questions.explanation: The procedure tests whether recorded items are present. Additional work addresses ownership and valuation.

questions.prompt: Inspecting whether purchase orders contain the required approval is primarily what kind of test?

choices.text: A test of controls.
A complete test of inventory valuation.
A financial statement opinion.
A confirmation of all vendor balances.

questions.explanation: The purpose is to test the operation of the approval control, not by itself to prove the reported amount.

questions.prompt: A sale shipped in January is recorded in December. Which assertion is most directly affected?

choices.text: Only legal ownership of the audit file.
Cutoff.
Only disclosure of audit fees.
No assertion because cash was collected later.

questions.explanation: The transaction is recorded in the wrong reporting period. Recognition terms and shipment evidence inform cutoff.

questions.prompt: A company physically holds goods owned by a consignor and includes them in its inventory. Which assertion is misstated?

choices.text: Existence, because the goods cannot be seen.
Accuracy only because all goods have zero value.
Rights and obligations.
No assertion; physical custody establishes ownership.

questions.explanation: The goods exist but the consignee does not own them. Custody is not ownership.

questions.prompt: When is a dual-purpose test appropriate?

choices.text: Whenever a document has a date.
Only when substantive testing is prohibited.
Whenever control exceptions are ignored.
When its design and evaluation support both the control and substantive objectives.

questions.explanation: Both objectives require appropriate evidence and separate evaluation; a label does not establish either.

questions.prompt: Choose the best procedure for each identified inventory and revenue risk. Risks: A: Recorded inventory may not exist. B: Shipped orders may be omitted from sales. C: Goods held on consignment may be included as owned inventory. D: January shipments may be recorded as December sales. Available evidence: Warehouse observations, shipping-document populations, contracts identifying ownership, and year-end sales entries are available. Select evidence relevant to the risk rather than the easiest document to obtain. Required: Procedure for A.

choices.text: Vouch recorded items to physical inventory
Trace only unrecorded orders
Inspect only payroll approvals
Confirm the auditor’s bank balance

questions.explanation: Vouching recorded quantities to goods addresses existence.

questions.prompt: Choose the best procedure for each identified inventory and revenue risk. Risks: A: Recorded inventory may not exist. B: Shipped orders may be omitted from sales. C: Goods held on consignment may be included as owned inventory. D: January shipments may be recorded as December sales. Available evidence: Warehouse observations, shipping-document populations, contracts identifying ownership, and year-end sales entries are available. Select evidence relevant to the risk rather than the easiest document to obtain. Required: Procedure for B.

choices.text: Select only recorded sales
Trace shipping documents to sales records
Inspect only the chart of accounts
Review dividend approvals

questions.explanation: Tracing an independent source population addresses omitted transactions.

questions.prompt: Choose the best procedure for each identified inventory and revenue risk. Risks: A: Recorded inventory may not exist. B: Shipped orders may be omitted from sales. C: Goods held on consignment may be included as owned inventory. D: January shipments may be recorded as December sales. Available evidence: Warehouse observations, shipping-document populations, contracts identifying ownership, and year-end sales entries are available. Select evidence relevant to the risk rather than the easiest document to obtain. Required: Assertion for C.

choices.text: Audit fee classification
Only arithmetic accuracy
Rights and obligations
No assertion

questions.explanation: Consigned goods may be physically present but not owned.

questions.prompt: Choose the best procedure for each identified inventory and revenue risk. Risks: A: Recorded inventory may not exist. B: Shipped orders may be omitted from sales. C: Goods held on consignment may be included as owned inventory. D: January shipments may be recorded as December sales. Available evidence: Warehouse observations, shipping-document populations, contracts identifying ownership, and year-end sales entries are available. Select evidence relevant to the risk rather than the easiest document to obtain. Required: Assertion for D.

choices.text: Only existence of the warehouse
Only audit documentation retention
No reporting-period issue
Cutoff

questions.explanation: January activity recognized in December misstates the reporting period.

questions.prompt: Which sampling approach most directly tests the frequency of missing approvals?

choices.text: A discounted cash flow valuation.
A compilation procedure.
A ratio of audit fees to sales.
Attribute sampling.

questions.explanation: Approval exceptions are control attributes, so the objective is a deviation rate.

questions.prompt: An auditor fails to recognize an exception in a document actually examined. Which risk is illustrated?

choices.text: Nonsampling risk.
Only sampling risk.
Only inherent risk.
A necessary consequence of statistical selection.

questions.explanation: The problem is execution or interpretation, not whether the selected sample represents the population.

questions.prompt: A homogeneous sample is overstated by $3,000 on recorded value of $60,000. Population recorded value is $900,000. Under ratio projection, what is projected overstatement?
questions.explanation: The ratio is 5%; 5% of $900,000 is $45,000 before sampling-risk allowances.

questions.prompt: All else equal, decreasing tolerable misstatement generally has what effect on substantive sample size?

choices.text: It always reduces sample size.
It eliminates sampling risk.
It increases the required sample size.
It makes population definition unnecessary.

questions.explanation: A tighter tolerance generally requires more evidence for a given assurance level.

questions.prompt: The evaluated upper deviation rate is 9% and the tolerable rate is 6%. What is the best conclusion?

choices.text: The control is supported because most items passed.
All substantive procedures can be omitted.
The difference can be ignored because it is under 10%.
The sample does not support the planned level of reliance.

questions.explanation: The evaluated deviation exceeds the tolerable rate; reassess reliance and the audit response.

questions.prompt: A team samples invoices from an incomplete ledger to test completeness of liabilities. What is the primary issue?

choices.text: The source population is inappropriate for detecting omitted liabilities.
The sample is automatically representative because it is random.
The confidence level cures the population problem.
Only the arithmetic in the projection matters.

questions.explanation: Random selection from incomplete records does not detect items absent from those records.

questions.prompt: Evaluate a control sample and a separate monetary sample using the specified methods. Control test: 80 approvals tested; 4 deviations found. The evaluated upper deviation rate is 8%. The tolerable rate is 6%. Substantive sample: A homogeneous population has recorded value $1,200,000. Sample recorded value is $80,000 and audited value is $76,000. Use ratio projection; sampling uncertainty must be evaluated separately. Required: Observed control deviation rate, as a percentage.

Evaluate a control sample and a separate monetary sample using the specified methods. Control test: 80 approvals tested; 4 deviations found. The evaluated upper deviation rate is 8%. The tolerable rate is 6%. Substantive sample: A homogeneous population has recorded value $1,200,000. Sample recorded value is $80,000 and audited value is $76,000. Use ratio projection; sampling uncertainty must be evaluated separately. Required: Conclusion using the upper deviation rate.

choices.text: Reliance is guaranteed
Ignore the upper rate
Planned reliance is not supported
No additional evaluation is needed

questions.explanation: The 8% upper rate exceeds the 6% tolerable rate.

questions.prompt: Evaluate a control sample and a separate monetary sample using the specified methods. Control test: 80 approvals tested; 4 deviations found. The evaluated upper deviation rate is 8%. The tolerable rate is 6%. Substantive sample: A homogeneous population has recorded value $1,200,000. Sample recorded value is $80,000 and audited value is $76,000. Use ratio projection; sampling uncertainty must be evaluated separately. Required: Sample monetary overstatement.
questions.explanation: $80,000 recorded less $76,000 audited = $4,000.

questions.prompt: Evaluate a control sample and a separate monetary sample using the specified methods. Control test: 80 approvals tested; 4 deviations found. A sales extract excludes all credit memos. What must the auditor address before relying on a net-sales analysis?

choices.text: The completeness and relevance of the extracted population.
Only the dashboard’s colors.
Only whether the file is a spreadsheet.
Nothing if the report totals are large.

questions.explanation: Omitted credit memos can bias net sales. Validate extraction criteria and reconcile to appropriate records.

questions.prompt: A building has 30 occupied units at $2,000 monthly for 12 months with no vacancies or concessions. What is expected annual rent?
What distinguishes a substantive analytical procedure from a general planning comparison?

choices.text: A colorful chart alone.
A management explanation with no corroboration.
An independently developed expectation with appropriate reliability and precision.
Use of the recorded balance as the only expectation.

questions.explanation: Substantive analytics require evidence capable of detecting a material difference at the intended assurance level.

questions.prompt: An inner join excludes customer accounts with no matching address. What risk does this introduce to a receivables test?

choices.text: An automatic overstatement of every remaining balance.
A guarantee of data integrity.
No risk because inner joins are always preferred.
An incomplete test population.

questions.explanation: Unmatched receivables can be silently omitted, so reconcile the joined population to the source.

questions.prompt: Management explains a significant variance as a price change. What should the auditor do?

choices.text: Corroborate the explanation using relevant evidence.
Accept it because it is mathematically possible.
Delete the analytical procedure.
Change the investigation threshold after seeing the difference.

questions.explanation: A plausible explanation needs supporting evidence, such as approved price changes and sales mix data.

questions.prompt: An AI tool generates an audit schedule. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: AI output is automatically independent external evidence.
The auditor remains responsible for validating the data and evaluating the output.
AI eliminates professional skepticism.
No documentation is needed if the output looks reasonable.

questions.explanation: Technology does not remove responsibility for reliable inputs, appropriate procedures, and supported conclusions.

questions.prompt: Evaluate an independently prepared revenue expectation and data-quality exceptions. Operational data: 50 units were occupied for all 12 months at $1,200 per month. There are no concessions. Recorded revenue is $690,000. The case uses a $15,000 investigation threshold. Extract review: The analyst’s SQL query omits unmatched customer IDs. A separate join duplicates records when a customer has multiple addresses. Management attributes all differences to seasonality without supporting evidence. Required: Expected annual revenue.

choices.text: Reconcile and correct population completeness and accuracy
Ignore them if the chart is clear
Increase only the font size
Assume all differences cancel

questions.explanation: Omissions and duplicate joins can bias the population and totals.

questions.prompt: Evaluate an independently prepared revenue expectation and data-quality exceptions. Operational data: 50 units were occupied for all 12 months at $1,200 per month. There are no concessions. Recorded revenue is $690,000. The case uses a $15,000 investigation threshold. Extract review: The analyst’s SQL query omits unmatched customer IDs. A separate join duplicates records when a customer has multiple addresses. Management attributes all differences to seasonality without supporting evidence. Required: Response to the seasonality explanation.

choices.text: Accept the statement without support
Obtain corroborating evidence and investigate the difference
Increase the threshold to $40,000 after the fact
Treat the expectation as a tax return

questions.explanation: The difference exceeds the threshold and requires supported investigation.

questions.prompt: A positive receivables confirmation receives no response. What is ordinarily appropriate?

choices.text: Treat silence as agreement.
Perform suitable alternative procedures and evaluate the remaining evidence gap.
Ask management to sign for the customer.
Delete the receivable from the sample without replacement or evaluation.

questions.explanation: Nonresponses require follow-up or alternatives when appropriate; silence is not affirmative evidence.

questions.prompt: Who should control the sending and receipt of audit confirmations?

choices.text: Client sales personnel alone.
The customer’s salesperson.
The auditor.
An unrelated investor.

questions.explanation: Auditor control supports the integrity of confirmation evidence.

questions.prompt: Which inventory test-count direction primarily addresses completeness?

choices.text: Select only recorded items and find them on the floor.
Read only the inventory valuation policy.
Confirm only the cash balance.
Select goods on the floor and trace them to count records.

questions.explanation: Floor-to-record testing can identify goods omitted from the count records.

questions.prompt: Which matter is not established merely by seeing inventory in a warehouse?

choices.text: Whether the entity owns the goods.
Whether the observed goods are physically present.
Whether the count takes place at that location.
Whether the goods can be inspected.

questions.explanation: Consigned or third-party goods may be physically present without ownership.

questions.prompt: A bank confirms its balance, but an old outstanding check appears on the client’s reconciliation. What should the auditor do?

choices.text: Accept the book balance solely because the bank replied.
Investigate the reconciling item rather than assuming the book balance is correct.
Ignore all reconciliation items after confirmation.
Treat every old check as a new liability automatically.

questions.explanation: Confirmation and reconciliation address different aspects of the balance and must be evaluated together.

questions.prompt: A confirmation response is forwarded by the client’s controller from an unverified email account. Which action is appropriate?

choices.text: Treat it as automatically independent evidence.
Assume electronic evidence is always invalid.
Authenticate the response and evaluate its reliability.
Ignore the source if the number matches.

questions.explanation: The source and transmission process affect reliability; investigate rather than blindly accept or categorically reject electronic evidence.

questions.prompt: Select the appropriate follow-up for four audit-evidence matters. Evidence received: A customer did not respond to a positive request. A response was forwarded through management from an unverified address. Goods counted include a clearly identified consignment from another company. A bank confirmation agrees to the bank statement, but the book reconciliation contains unusual old transfers. Audit approach: Evaluate each item’s reliability and assertion implications. No alternative procedure has yet been performed, and the balances are material. Required: Follow-up for the nonresponse.

choices.text: Treat silence as agreement
Accept a controller signature
Ignore the selected item
Perform suitable alternative procedures

questions.explanation: A positive request requires appropriate evidence rather than silence.

questions.prompt: Select the appropriate follow-up for four audit-evidence matters. Evidence received: A customer did not respond to a positive request. A response was forwarded through management from an unverified address. Goods counted include a clearly identified consignment from another company. A bank confirmation agrees to the bank statement, but the book reconciliation contains unusual old transfers. Audit approach: Evaluate each item’s reliability and assertion implications. No alternative procedure has yet been performed, and the balances are material. Required: Follow-up for the forwarded response.

choices.text: Authenticate source and transmission
Assume independence
Reject every electronic response
Ignore the source

questions.explanation: Reliability must be established in the circumstances.

questions.prompt: Select the appropriate follow-up for four audit-evidence matters. Evidence received: A customer did not respond to a positive request. A response was forwarded through management from an unverified address. Goods counted include a clearly identified consignment from another company. A bank confirmation agrees to the bank statement, but the book reconciliation contains unusual old transfers. Audit approach: Evaluate each item’s reliability and assertion implications. No alternative procedure has yet been performed, and the balances are material. Required: Assertion implicated by the consignment.

choices.text: Only audit timing
Rights and obligations
No assertion
Only depreciation

questions.explanation: Physical custody does not establish ownership.

questions.prompt: Select the appropriate follow-up for four audit-evidence matters. Evidence received: A customer did not respond to a positive request. A response was forwarded through management from an unverified address. Goods counted include a clearly identified consignment from another company. A bank confirmation agrees to the bank statement, but the book reconciliation contains unusual old transfers. Audit approach: Evaluate each item’s reliability and assertion implications. No alternative procedure has yet been performed, and the balances are material. Required: Follow-up for old bank transfers.

choices.text: Rely only on the confirmed bank balance
Remove the reconciliation from the file
Investigate and support the reconciling items
Assume all transfers are immaterial

questions.explanation: Unusual reconciling items can affect the book cash balance and cutoff.

questions.prompt: A January payment of $35,000 relates entirely to services received in December. No year-end accrual exists. What does it indicate?

choices.text: A January-only expense in every framework.
No liability because payment was after year-end.
A potential $35,000 unrecorded year-end liability and expense.
An automatic $35,000 asset.

questions.explanation: Recognition depends on the obligation and service period, not merely the cash-payment date.

questions.prompt: Which source is useful in a search for unrecorded liabilities?

choices.text: Only the recorded year-end liability list.
Only the auditor’s engagement letter.
Only the common-stock register.
Subsequent cash disbursements and supporting invoices.

questions.explanation: A source outside the possibly incomplete liability ledger can reveal omitted obligations.

questions.prompt: Management changes an estimate assumption solely to meet an earnings target. What is a key audit concern?

choices.text: Management bias in the estimate.
Only the number of decimal places.
A guarantee that the estimate is immaterial.
An automatic permission to stop testing.

questions.explanation: The motive and unsupported assumption can indicate bias and require further evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which is an appropriate audit approach to an accounting estimate?

choices.text: Accept management’s point estimate because estimates are uncertain.
Develop an independent expectation or range using relevant evidence.
Use an unrelated industry number without analysis.
Assume all subsequent events adjust the estimate.

questions.explanation: An independent expectation can provide evidence when its assumptions and data are relevant and reliable.

questions.prompt: Management refuses permission for necessary inquiry of legal counsel about material litigation. What should the auditor evaluate?

choices.text: Only whether the law firm is expensive.
Whether the auditor can guarantee the court outcome.
The resulting evidence limitation and its reporting implications.
Nothing if management signs a broad representation.

questions.explanation: A representation does not replace necessary evidence; evaluate materiality and pervasiveness of the limitation.

questions.prompt: A large year-end related-party sale has no clear business purpose and includes a side agreement. What is appropriate?

choices.text: Accept the invoice alone.
Exclude the sale from all testing.
Assume related-party sales are always prohibited.
Investigate substance, recognition, disclosure, and fraud implications.

questions.explanation: The auditor must understand the full arrangement and its financial-reporting implications.

questions.prompt: Evaluate a subsequent-disbursement schedule and two judgmental matters. Payments after year-end: Payment A: $22,000 for December services, not accrued. Payment B: $18,000 for January services. Payment C: $31,000 for goods received before year-end, not accrued. All amounts are valid obligations. Other matters: Management sets an unsupported reserve assumption to meet a profit target and refuses necessary legal-counsel inquiry about material litigation. Required: Total omitted year-end liabilities from A, B, and C.
questions.explanation: Only December services and goods already received create the described year-end omissions: $22,000 + $31,000.

questions.prompt: Evaluate a subsequent-disbursement schedule and two judgmental matters. Payments after year-end: Payment A: $22,000 for December services, not accrued. Payment B: $18,000 for January services. Payment C: $31,000 for goods received before year-end, not accrued. All amounts are valid obligations. Other matters: Management sets an unsupported reserve assumption to meet a profit target and refuses necessary legal-counsel inquiry about material litigation. Required: Amount belonging only to January based on these facts.
questions.explanation: Payment B relates to January services.

questions.prompt: Evaluate a subsequent-disbursement schedule and two judgmental matters. Payments after year-end: Payment A: $22,000 for December services, not accrued. choices.text: Only a documentation font issue
No issue because estimates are subjective
Unsupported management bias
Automatic assurance from the target

questions.explanation: The assumption is driven by an earnings target rather than evidence.

Payment B: $18,000 for January services. Payment C: $31,000 for goods received before year-end, not accrued. All amounts are valid obligations. Required: Consequence to evaluate from legal-counsel refusal.

choices.text: A guarantee the lawsuit will be won
Automatic immateriality
Permission to omit disclosure
An evidence limitation

questions.explanation: Necessary evidence cannot be replaced solely by management representations.

questions.prompt: A custodian confirms the number of securities held. Which matter generally needs separate evidence?

choices.text: Whether the confirmation has a date.
Whether the securities were described in the response.
Whether the auditor received a response.
Whether the year-end recorded fair value is appropriate.

questions.explanation: Quantity and custody evidence do not automatically establish fair value.

questions.prompt: An entity holds 2,000 units. The relevant year-end fair value is $47 per unit, but it records $100,000. What is the indicated valuation difference?

choices.text: $6,000 overstatement.
$6,000 understatement.
$94,000 overstatement.
No difference.

questions.explanation: 2,000 × $47 = $94,000; recorded value exceeds it by $6,000.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes sufficiency and appropriateness?

choices.text: Sufficiency concerns the fee; appropriateness concerns the report length.
Sufficiency concerns quantity; appropriateness concerns evidence quality.
Both refer only to the number of documents.
Both eliminate the need for professional judgment.

questions.explanation: Quality includes relevance and reliability, while sufficiency addresses the amount of evidence.

questions.prompt: Two reliable-looking sources provide conflicting prices for a material investment. What is appropriate?

choices.text: Select the price closest to management’s preference.
Average the numbers without evaluating relevance.
Investigate the difference and obtain evidence supporting the measurement.
Ignore both because they conflict.

questions.explanation: Evaluate source relevance, instrument comparability, date, and pricing assumptions before concluding.

questions.prompt: Management signs a representation that all investments are properly valued, but supporting model data is unavailable. What follows?

choices.text: The signature resolves every evidence gap.
The model must be correct if its output is material.
No opinion consideration is ever needed.
The representation does not replace necessary valuation evidence.

questions.explanation: Representations are necessary in many audits but are not substitutes for other reasonably expected evidence.

questions.prompt: A material investment is pledged as collateral. What audit consideration arises beyond existence?

choices.text: Appropriate restriction or pledge disclosure.
Only the auditor’s independence from the custodian.
Automatic derecognition of the investment.
No reporting consequence in any case.

questions.explanation: Restrictions and pledges may require disclosure; confirmation alone does not settle presentation.
